sysd-reliab-091.title: Disaster recovery: running again after the site is lost
sysd-reliab-091.text:
Disaster recovery starts from a pessimistic assumption: the primary site cannot be recovered right away. It is the process of regaining access to infrastructure and systems after a natural disaster, cyber attack or other business disruption. Disasters come in three broad kinds: natural hazards such as floods and earthquakes, and technological hazards such as system failures and utility disruptions. The third kind is human-caused threats such as cyber attacks, sabotage and war.

The method leans on {{ref:sysd-scale-043}}. Data and computer processing are copied to an off-premises location that the disaster does not affect, and the business restores data and services to that secondary site. When servers go down, it recovers lost data from the second location and, ideally, moves its processing there to keep operating. Policies, tools and procedures apply to the IT systems behind critical business functions, which makes disaster recovery a subset of {{ref:sysd-reliab-184}}.

The payoff is less interruption and downtime, limited damage, faster restoration and customers who stay. Some regulators do not leave it optional. In US healthcare, the HIPAA Security Rule requires disaster recovery plans, plans for keeping copies of data, and periodic testing of contingency procedures. Singh notes that disaster recovery is seldom discussed in system design interviews but is worth a basic understanding.

sysd-reliab-189.title: Backup: a copy kept somewhere else
sysd-reliab-189.text: A backup is a copy of computer data taken and stored elsewhere so it can be used to restore the original after a data loss event. It recovers data lost to deletion or corruption, or data from an earlier time. It is a simple form of {{ref:sysd-reliab-091}}, though not every backup system can rebuild a cluster or database server. Backup differs from {{ref:sysd-scale-043}} because the saved copy stays unchanged for a long period. Online storage starts a restore in milliseconds, off-line storage is immune to online failure modes, and a vault off-site protects against site-specific disasters. Deduplication stores one copy of redundant data, and compression shrinks it further. Encrypting backup media mitigates loss or theft, but encryption is CPU intensive and only as secure as the key management policy. Checksums and dry runs check that the copy is reliable.

sysd-reliab-205.title: Data integrity: why lost data and a dead service look alike
sysd-reliab-205.text: To a user, lost data, corrupted data and a service that stays unavailable for too long all look the same. Data integrity is the accuracy and consistency of data over its lifetime, and it means that services remain accessible to users with accurate data. Integrity without regular availability is effectively the same as having no data. Google suggests 24 hours as a starting threshold for unavailability that is too long. Each service has its own uptime and integrity needs. A 99.99% uptime target allows about an hour of downtime a year. But 99.99% good bytes in a 2 GB artifact means up to 200 KB garbled, which is catastrophic. The secret to superior integrity is proactive detection plus rapid repair and recovery. A corrupted artifact detected and fixed within half an hour still leaves it 99.99% available that year. The right mix trades uptime against integrity and depends on how an application balances uptime, latency, scale, velocity and privacy.

sysd-reliab-201.title: Monitoring: real-time numbers that say when something breaks
sysd-reliab-201.text: Teams that practice {{ref:sysd-reliab-104}}, or SRE, avoid any situation that requires someone to stare at a screen to watch for problems. Monitoring is collecting, processing, aggregating and displaying real-time quantitative data about a system, such as query counts and types, error counts and types, processing times and server lifetimes. It lets a system say when it is broken or about to break; when it cannot fix itself, a human investigates, mitigates and finds the root cause. Teams monitor to analyze long-term trends, compare over time or between experiment groups, raise alerts, build dashboards and debug ad hoc. A dashboard is a prebuilt summary view of a service's core metrics, normally including the {{ref:sysd-reliab-202}}. Alerts are notifications for humans, classified as tickets, email alerts and pages. Simpler and faster monitoring works best, because monitoring that grows complex becomes fragile and a maintenance burden. The rules that catch real incidents most often should stay simple, predictable and reliable.

sysd-reliab-099.title: Service level indicator: the number that measures a service
sysd-reliab-099.text: Before anyone can promise a level of service, someone has to measure it. A service level indicator (SLI) is a measure of the service level a provider delivers to a customer. It is a carefully defined quantitative measure of some aspect of that level. Request latency is the key SLI for most services. Error rate, a fraction of requests, and throughput in requests per second are also common, along with availability. Storage systems add durability, and pipelines add end-to-end latency. A simple web service might define availability as the ratio of successful responses to the total valid requests received. Measurements are usually aggregated: raw data is collected over a window and turned into a rate, average or percentile. Ideally an SLI measures the service level of interest directly, but sometimes only a proxy exists. Client-side latency matters most to users yet may only be measurable at the server. SLIs form the basis of the targets in {{ref:sysd-reliab-103}}, which in turn form the basis of {{ref:sysd-reliab-100}}.

sysd-reliab-103.title: Service level objective: the target a service promises to hit
sysd-reliab-103.text:
In simple terms, service-level objectives are targets for how often a service may fail or not operate properly while users are still not meaningfully upset. More formally, an SLO is a target value or range of values for a service level, measured by a {{ref:sysd-reliab-099}}. SLOs are formed by setting goals for such indicators. An availability SLO may be the expected value of an availability indicator over a prescribed duration, for example four weeks. Typical SLOs cover availability, throughput, frequency, response time or quality.

A well-formed SLO states an achievement value, a target measurement, a measurement period, and where and how it is measured. One example is 90% of helpdesk calls answered in under 20 seconds over one month. Others are an application available 99.95% of the time over a year, or 85% of TCP replies within 1.5 seconds and 99.5% within 4 seconds over a month.

An SLO is a key element of an {{ref:sysd-reliab-100}}: each one is an individual promise within it, and the specific goal the service must meet to comply. SLOs give a quantitative definition of the service level a customer can expect, and they are agreed to measure the provider's performance and avoid disputes from misunderstanding. They should always be simple, clearly defined and easy to measure, so it is clear whether the objective is being met. Companies also set internal SLOs for internal services that depend on each other, especially those practicing {{ref:sysd-reliab-104}}.

sysd-reliab-100.title: Service-level agreement: the promise written into a contract
sysd-reliab-100.text: A service-level agreement can cost a provider money. An SLA is an agreement, typically a binding contract, between a service provider and a customer. It sets the quality, availability and responsibilities of a service as contract terms. In outsourcing it is negotiated upfront and may carry financial penalties and a right to terminate if its metrics are consistently missed. It is often written by the business or legal team. It often contains service-level objectives for defined service level indicators, such as mean time between failures, mean time to repair, uptime and turnaround time. Unlike traditional contracts, SLAs often require the parties to meet regularly, apply rewards and penalties for performance, and leave room for periodic revision. They exist at different levels: customer-based for one customer group, service-based for all customers of a service, and multilevel when one SLA addresses different customer sets in layers. Large organizations also keep internal SLAs between units, one as customer and one as provider.

sysd-reliab-093.title: Recovery point objective: how much recent data you can lose
sysd-reliab-093.text: If the plan is to restore the last available backup, the recovery point objective is simply the interval between such backups. The RPO is the maximum acceptable amount of time since the last recovery point, that is, the longest interval of data loss tolerated. It measures time, not the quantity of data lost. The existing backup regime does not set it; the {{ref:sysd-reliab-185}} sets it for each service. When the RPO is measured in minutes, off-site mirrored backups must be maintained continuously, because a daily off-site backup will not suffice. When data must go off-site, the period in which data might be lost may start when backups are prepared, not when they are secured off-site. A data synchronization point is where a backup is completed. Update processing halts during the disk-to-disk copy, and the backup reflects the data as of that copy, not when it reaches tape. Sending synchronous copies to an offsite mirror allows for most unforeseen events.

sysd-reliab-190.title: Backup methods: full, incremental, differential and continuous
sysd-reliab-190.text:
Backup methods differ in what each backup copies. The options are complete data, changes since the last full backup, changes since the last backup of any kind, or every change as it happens. A full backup holds complete copies of the source data at specific points in time. A system image records a known good configuration, but it suits deploying a standard setup more than ongoing backup. An incremental backup stores only data changed since a reference point, usually a full backup. A restore starts from the last full backup and applies the incrementals, and some systems build a synthetic full from them. A differential backup saves data changed since the last full backup, so a restore needs at most two backups, but each differential takes longer as changes accumulate. The two differ in their reference point. Incrementals copy changes since the most recent backup of any type. Differentials copy changes since the last full backup, whatever differentials came between.

A reverse incremental keeps a recent mirror of the source plus the differences needed to rebuild earlier states, by periodically synchronizing the full backup with the live copy. Continuous data protection instantly saves every change and allows restoring to any point in time. Near-CDP takes incremental backups at intervals such as every 15 minutes, so restores only reach an interval boundary. At the careless end, an unstructured repository is a stack of media with minimal information about what was backed up. It is the easiest to implement but unlikely to be highly recoverable, because it lacks automation.

sysd-reliab-092.title: Recovery time objective: how long you can stay down
sysd-reliab-092.text: How long can an application or network stay offline after a disaster? The recovery time objective is the answer: the maximum acceptable delay between an interruption of service and its restoration. It sets the acceptable window during which a service may be unavailable. When organizations plan for business continuity, process owners set the RTO during a {{ref:sysd-reliab-185}}, including time frames for alternate or manual workarounds. A stated objective is not proof. The business continuity group runs timed rehearsals to determine and refine the recovery time actual, the critical metric against which the RTO is checked. Together, the RTO and the {{ref:sysd-reliab-093}} measure tolerable performance: time lost from normal business functioning, and data lost or not backed up during that period. Both must be balanced against business risk and the other system design criteria. Recovery metrics are often used alongside failure metrics: mean time between failures, mean time to first failure, mean time to repair and mean down time.

sysd-reliab-095.title: Hot, warm and cold sites: how ready is the standby?
sysd-reliab-095.text:
A standby site can be running, nearly ready or barely started, and the three states have names. A backup site is hot if it operates before a disaster. It is warm if it is ready to begin operating, and cold if it needs substantial work to begin operating. A robust disaster recovery strategy starts from two benchmarks, the {{ref:sysd-reliab-092}} and the {{ref:sysd-reliab-093}}, and picks a standby tier that meets them.

In a cold site the organization sets up only basic infrastructure in a second site. A hot site keeps up-to-date copies of data at all times; it is time-consuming to set up and costs more than a cold site, but dramatically reduces downtime. Four standby tiers put numbers on the choice. Backup and restore means regular backups of data and systems. Typical RTO runs from several hours to a few days, and RPO from a few hours up to the last successful backup. Pilot light keeps crucial components ready to activate so it can scale rapidly. Its RTO is typically a few minutes to several hours, and its RPO depends on how often data is synchronized. Warm standby is a semi-active environment with current data. Its RTO is within a few minutes to hours, and its RPO is up to the last few minutes or hours. A hot site or multi-site configuration is a fully operational duplicate environment running in parallel with the primary. Its RTO is almost immediate, often a few minutes, and its RPO is usually a few seconds.

sysd-reliab-206.title: Defense in depth: layers against data loss
sysd-reliab-206.text: No silver bullet covers the many combinations of ways data can be lost. Defense in depth answers with multiple layers, each guarding against progressively less common loss scenarios. The first layer is {{ref:sysd-reliab-207}}, the second is backups and their recovery methods, and the third is regular data validation for early detection. Replication cuts across all layers and is occasionally useful for recovery in specific scenarios, but recovery plans should not rely on it. Even a bulletproof system is susceptible to bugs and operator error. Services must therefore detect integrity issues quickly for them to be fixable, and protection mechanisms must be assumed able to fail too. Large-scale integrity needs several complementary but uncoupled practices, each offering a high degree of protection on its own. Many disks and a fast network for replication do not remove the need for layers, because multiple layers guard against breakdown or compromise of any single protection mechanism.

sysd-reliab-210.title: Replication is not backup: it copies your mistakes too
sysd-reliab-210.text: A replica will faithfully copy your mistake. Datastores that automatically sync replicas push a corrupt row or an errant delete to every copy, likely before the problem can be isolated, so replication is not recoverability. Replication gives data locality and protection from a site-specific disaster. It cannot protect against many sources of data loss, so it is a flawed answer to being asked whether you have a backup. Nonserving copies in another format, such as frequent database exports, guard against user errors and application bugs but not lower-layer losses. They also add the risk of bugs in data conversion. Diversity is key: protecting against failure at one layer needs data on diverse components at that layer, and a disk driver bug is unlikely to affect tape drives. Freshness and restore speed compete with comprehensive protection. Replication takes seconds, exporting a database snapshot to the filesystem about 40 minutes, and a full filesystem backup hours, with restores about as slow. Where replicating every backup is infeasible, stagger backups across independently failing sites.

sysd-reliab-207.title: Soft deletion: a grace period before data is destroyed
sysd-reliab-207.text: When velocity is high and privacy matters, application bugs cause most data loss and corruption. Undeleting data for a limited time then becomes the primary defense against permanent inadvertent loss. Soft deletion marks deleted data immediately, making it unusable except by the application's administrative code paths, and destroys it after a reasonable delay. It starts when a user empties the trash, and a support tool lets authorized administrators undelete items. It also helps against account hijackers who delete the original user's data. The delay depends on policy, law, storage cost and pricing; common choices are 15, 30, 45 or 60 days. Since most hijacking and integrity issues surface within 60 days, longer delays have a weak case. Lazy deletion is soft deletion controlled by the storage system, which keeps deleted data up to a few weeks. The most devastating deletions come from developers unfamiliar with deletion-related code, especially batch pipelines, so interfaces should hinder bypassing soft deletion.

sysd-reliab-223.title: Backend subsetting: each client talks to a few servers
sysd-reliab-223.text: Every connection costs memory and CPU at both ends, and too many connections per client or per backend waste resources for little gain. Subsetting limits the pool of backend tasks a client connects to. A typical subset size is 20 to 100 backends, with larger subsets when clients are far fewer than backends or send bursts. The selection algorithm should assign backends uniformly, since overloading one by 10% means overprovisioning all by 10%. It should also minimize connection churn across restarts, failures and resizes. Random subsetting works poorly. With 300 clients, 300 backends and subsets of 10%, the least loaded backend gets 50% of average load and the most loaded 150%. Deterministic subsetting divides clients into rounds, so each round assigns every backend to exactly one client, using a shuffled backend list. A different seed per round spreads a failed backend's load over all remaining backends instead of only its subset. In the 300-client example with subsets of 10 backends, every backend gets exactly the same number of connections. In general the counts differ by at most 1.

sysd-reliab-222.title: Lame duck state: asking clients to stop sending requests
sysd-reliab-222.text: A backend can be perfectly able to serve and still tell its clients to go away. In lame duck state it is listening and able to serve. But it explicitly asks clients to stop sending requests, and it broadcasts that fact to all its active clients. From a client's view, a backend is in one of three conditions: healthy and processing requests, refusing connections, or in lame duck state. Inactive clients still send periodic UDP health checks, so the news reaches every client, typically within 1 or 2 round trips. The state simplifies clean shutdown. On shutdown the task gets SIGTERM, enters lame duck state and lets ongoing requests drain. After a configured interval, by rule of thumb 10s to 150s, it exits cleanly or is killed. Requests in flight see no errors, which eases code pushes, maintenance and restarts after machine failures. A simpler alternative, flow control, treats a backend as unhealthy once a client's active requests reach a limit, and 100 is reasonable for most. It protects only against extreme overload and can leave all backends unreachable.

sysd-reliab-224.title: Limits of simple round robin: uneven load despite fair turns
sysd-reliab-224.text: Simple round robin looks fair, yet it can leave one task with up to twice the CPU load of another. It sends each client's requests in turn to the connectable, non-lame-duck backends in its subset, and it beats random selection. Several things break the evenness. Clients issue requests at different rates, especially when very different processes share backends, so with small subsets the backends of the busiest clients are naturally more loaded. Query costs vary widely. The most expensive requests may use 1000x or more CPU than the cheapest. One Java backend averages about 15 ms of CPU per query, yet some queries need up to 10 seconds. Machine diversity means the same request is different work on different CPUs. Antagonistic neighbors can change performance by up to 20%, and task restarts need extra resources for minutes. The cost is capacity: you may reserve 1,000 CPUs for a service in a datacenter yet be unable to use more than, say, 700.

sysd-reliab-220.title: Virtual IP load balancing: one address, many machines
sysd-reliab-220.text: Users see one regular IP address. A virtual IP address is shared across many devices rather than assigned to one network interface, and a network load balancer forwards packets to a machine behind it. It hides how many machines there are, so operators can add or upgrade them unseen. Always picking the least loaded backend breaks down for stateful protocols. They need the same backend for a whole connection, so the balancer must track every connection passing through it. The stateless alternative hashes parts of a packet into a connection ID and selects the backend from it. All packets of a connection then reach the same backend without stored state. But take the ID modulo the number of backends N, and removing one backend changes N to N-1. That remaps almost every packet. When backends share no state, nearly all connections reset. {{ref:sysd-scale-078}}, proposed in 1997, keeps the mapping relatively stable when backends come and go. Simple connection tracking is usually enough, falling back to consistent hashing during an ongoing denial of service attack.

sysd-reliab-196.title: Error budget: how much failure a service may spend
sysd-reliab-196.text: Insisting on meeting objectives 100% of the time slows innovation and deployment, and it needs costly, overly conservative solutions. An error budget is the alternative: the rate at which a service may miss its SLOs. It gives an objective measure of how unreliable the service is allowed to be within a period. Product management defines an SLO, a neutral monitoring system measures actual uptime, and the difference is the unreliability budget left for the quarter. Take an SLO of serving 99.999% of queries per quarter. The error budget is then a 0.001% failure rate, and a problem failing 0.0002% of expected queries spends 20% of the quarterly budget. Developers are judged on velocity and SREs on reliability, so they pull in opposite directions. The budget is an objective agreed metric that removes politics and gives both a common incentive. It works as a control loop on release velocity. Releases continue while SLOs are met and halt when the budget is spent, and then testing and resilience work is added. Network outages and datacenter failures also consume the budget.

sysd-reliab-197.title: Reliability versus cost: when more nines make things worse
sysd-reliab-197.text: A user on a smartphone that is 99% reliable cannot tell a 99.99% service from a 99.999% one. Other components, such as the cellular network, dominate what the user experiences. That is why, past a certain point, more reliability makes things worse for the service and its users. Extreme reliability limits feature development and delivery and sharply raises cost. Cost does not rise linearly, since an incremental improvement in reliability may cost 100x more than the previous increment. It has two dimensions: redundant machines and equipment, for maintenance windows or parity blocks, and the opportunity cost of engineers reducing risk instead of building user-visible features. SRE manages reliability by managing risk as a continuum, weighing cost against benefit per service. The goal is reliable enough but no more. An availability target such as 99.99% is both a minimum and a maximum. Exceeding it by much wastes chances to add features, clean up technical debt or cut costs.

openers.service-levels-and-disaster-recovery: To a user, lost data, corrupted data and a service that stays unavailable for too long all look the same. This chapter is about preventing that and about recovering when it happens. It begins with the promises a provider makes, measured by indicators, set as objectives and written into agreements. It then turns to disaster recovery, the process of regaining access to infrastructure and systems after a natural disaster, cyber attack or other disruption, and to the copies of data that make recovery possible. Along the way come the layers that protect data and the real-time numbers that say when a system is in trouble.
